quests.title: Legion on the March
quests.story: Left, right, left, right! The legion is marching into Britain. Grab your shield and learn what it took to be a Roman soldier.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the shield with the right answer.
quests.hint: Think about how the Roman army stayed so organised: ranks, training, teamwork and special kit.

questions.ask: What was a Roman foot soldier who was a Roman citizen called?
questions.fact: Legionaries usually served in the army for 20 to 25 years.

questions.ask: Which officer was in charge of a group of about 80 soldiers?
questions.fact: Despite the name, a centurion's group, called a century, had 80 men, not 100.

questions.ask: What was the Roman 'tortoise' shield formation called?
questions.fact: Soldiers held their shields above and around them, like a tortoise's shell.

questions.ask: What was the legionary's short sword called?
questions.fact: Its short blade suited fighting in tight, close lines of soldiers.

questions.ask: What was a pilum?
questions.fact: Its thin iron neck bent when it struck, so it could not be thrown back.

questions.ask: What was the large, curved Roman shield called?
questions.fact: It was made of layers of wood covered with leather, with a metal boss in the middle.

questions.ask: What was a legionary's body armour often made from?
questions.fact: We call strip armour lorica segmentata; other soldiers wore chain mail.

questions.ask: About how many soldiers were in a Roman legion?
questions.fact: For most of Roman times, three legions were based in Britain.

questions.ask: What were soldiers who were not Roman citizens called?
questions.fact: Auxiliaries could become Roman citizens when they retired after 25 years.

questions.ask: What did a legion build each night when it was on the march?
questions.fact: Soldiers dug a ditch and bank around neat rows of tents, ready by nightfall.

questions.ask: About how far could Roman soldiers march in a day?
questions.fact: They carried heavy packs with tools, food and cooking pots as they marched.

questions.ask: What were the soldiers' studded sandals called?
questions.fact: Iron nails in the soles gave grip and helped the sandals last on long marches.

quests.title: Romans in Britain

skill.name: Key events in Roman Britain in order
skill.subject: history

quests.story: Hold your torch high and walk through nearly 500 years of Roman Britain, from Julius Caesar's first landing to the day the army left.
quests.instruction: Tap the Roman event that happened first.
quests.hint: Remember BC dates come before AD dates, and a bigger BC number is longer ago.

events.label: Caesar's first visit
events.fact: Julius Caesar landed in Kent but soon sailed back to Gaul, which is now France.

events.label: Caesar returns
events.fact: This time he beat the British leader Cassivellaunus, but still did not stay.

events.label: Claudius invades
events.fact: About 40,000 soldiers landed, and Emperor Claudius came to see the victory.

events.label: Caratacus captured
events.fact: He was taken to Rome, where his brave speech made Claudius spare his life.

events.label: Boudica's revolt
events.fact: Boudica, queen of the Iceni, led a huge uprising against Roman rule.

events.label: Fishbourne Palace
events.fact: This grand building in Sussex had beautiful mosaic floors and formal gardens.

events.label: Hadrian's Wall begun
events.fact: Emperor Hadrian visited Britain and ordered a wall across the north.

events.label: Antonine Wall begun
events.fact: This turf wall across Scotland was left after only about 20 years.

events.label: Constantine in York
events.fact: Constantine was declared emperor at York and later supported Christianity.

events.label: Romans leave Britain
events.fact: The army was needed elsewhere, so Britons had to defend themselves.

quests.title: Hadrian's Wall Watch
quests.story: Night has fallen on the wall and it's your turn on watch! Light your lantern and find out about life on the edge of the Roman Empire.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the lantern with the right answer.
quests.hint: Imagine being a soldier far from home, guarding a long wall that crossed the whole of northern England.

questions.ask: Which Roman emperor ordered the wall to be built?
questions.fact: Hadrian visited Britain in AD 122, the year building began.

questions.ask: About how long is Hadrian's Wall?
questions.fact: It ran coast to coast, from Wallsend on the River Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway.

questions.ask: What were the small forts placed every Roman mile along the wall?
questions.fact: Between each pair of milecastles stood two small watchtowers called turrets.

questions.ask: Which fort near the wall is famous for its writing tablets?
questions.fact: Vindolanda was built before the wall and stands just south of it.

questions.ask: What were the Vindolanda tablets made from?
questions.fact: Written in ink, they are some of the oldest handwritten documents found in Britain.

questions.ask: In one tablet, Claudia Severa invites her friend to what?
questions.fact: It is thought to be the oldest known writing in Latin by a woman.

questions.ask: What do historians think was one reason the wall was built?
questions.fact: Soldiers could watch who crossed the frontier and collect taxes on trade.

questions.ask: Where did many soldiers on the wall come from?
questions.fact: Soldiers came from places such as modern Belgium, Spain, Syria and North Africa.

questions.ask: What was Hadrian's Wall built from?
questions.fact: The western part was first built of turf and later rebuilt in stone.

questions.ask: Which country is all of Hadrian's Wall in today?
questions.fact: Many people think it marks the Scottish border, but it lies wholly in England.

questions.ask: What was dug along the north side of the wall?
questions.fact: Behind the wall, a bigger earthwork called the Vallum marked the army's zone.

questions.ask: About how long did it take to build most of the wall?
questions.fact: Most of the work was done by soldiers from the three legions in Britain.

quests.title: Roman or Celt?
quests.story: The market is busy and everything is muddled up! Sort each thing into the right basket: did it belong to the Romans or the Celts?
quests.instruction: Is it Roman or Celtic? Tap the right basket.
quests.hint: Think about who brought towns, Latin and stone buildings, and who already lived in Britain's roundhouses.

questions.ask: Villas with mosaic floors
questions.fact: Mosaics were pictures made from thousands of tiny coloured tiles called tesserae.

questions.ask: Long, straight roads
questions.fact: The Romans built about 2,000 miles of roads in Britain to move soldiers quickly.

questions.ask: Speaking and writing Latin
questions.fact: Latin was the language of the Roman Empire and its laws.

questions.ask: Public bath houses
questions.fact: Romans went to the baths to wash, relax, exercise and chat with friends.

questions.ask: Wearing togas
questions.fact: Only Roman citizens were allowed to wear the toga.

questions.ask: Towns with a forum
questions.fact: The forum was a market square at the heart of every Roman town.

questions.ask: Living in roundhouses
questions.fact: Roundhouses had thatched roofs and a fire in the middle for warmth and cooking.

questions.ask: Druid priests
questions.fact: Druids were religious leaders, teachers and judges for the Celtic tribes.

questions.ask: Gold torcs worn by chiefs
questions.fact: A torc was a heavy neck ring that showed a person was rich and important.

questions.ask: Painting skin blue with woad
questions.fact: Julius Caesar wrote that Britons coloured themselves blue with woad.

questions.ask: Fighting from chariots
questions.fact: Caesar was amazed by British chariot drivers, who could leap out and run along the pole.

questions.ask: Stories passed on by word of mouth
questions.fact: The Celts in Britain did not write books, so they remembered stories and laws.

quests.title: What the Romans Gave Us

skill.name: What the Romans left behind in Britain
skill.subject: history

quests.story: What have the Romans ever done for us? Quite a lot, it turns out! Collect gold coins as you discover what they left behind in Britain.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the coin with the right answer.
quests.hint: Think about things we still use today, like roads, towns, words and even the names of months.

questions.ask: What were Roman roads famous for?
questions.fact: Many modern roads, like parts of the A5, follow the old Roman Watling Street.

questions.ask: What did the Romans call London?
questions.fact: The Romans built the first bridge across the Thames in London.

questions.ask: What did the Romans call the town of Bath?
questions.fact: Hot spring water still bubbles up there at about 46°C.

questions.ask: What was the Roman system of underfloor heating called?
questions.fact: Hot air from a fire flowed under floors held up by stacks of tiles.

questions.ask: Which month is named after Julius Caesar?
questions.fact: August is named after the first Roman emperor, Augustus.

questions.ask: Which language did the Romans speak?
questions.fact: English words like 'video', 'audio' and 'animal' come straight from Latin.

questions.ask: What did the Romans build to carry fresh water to towns?
questions.fact: Water flowed gently downhill along channels, sometimes over tall bridges.

questions.ask: Whose head was shown on most Roman coins?
questions.fact: Coins spread the emperor's face and name across the whole empire.

questions.ask: Which religion began to spread in Britain in later Roman times?
questions.fact: Emperor Constantine allowed Christians to worship freely in AD 313.

questions.ask: The word 'plumber' comes from the Latin for which metal?
questions.fact: Romans made water pipes from lead, which they called plumbum.

questions.ask: What was the open square at the centre of a Roman town called?
questions.fact: Around the forum stood shops, offices and the basilica, a kind of town hall.

questions.ask: Town names ending in '-chester' come from a Latin word meaning what?
questions.fact: Manchester, Lancaster and Gloucester all grew up around Roman forts.

quests.title: Athens or Sparta?
quests.story: Two great Greek city-states, two very different ways of life! Help the messenger sort out which city each fact belongs to.
quests.instruction: Athens or Sparta? Tap the shield of the right city.
quests.hint: Athens loved ideas, art and voting; Sparta put fighting and tough training first.

questions.ask: Citizens voted in a democracy
questions.fact: Athens had the world's first democracy, though only men who were citizens could vote.

questions.ask: Home of the philosopher Socrates
questions.fact: Philosophers like Socrates and Plato asked big questions about life.

questions.ask: Built the Parthenon temple
questions.fact: The Parthenon was built on the Acropolis, a rocky hill above the city.

questions.ask: Named after the goddess Athena
questions.fact: The Greeks told a myth that Athena won the city in a contest with Poseidon.

questions.ask: Famous for plays and theatres
questions.fact: Huge crowds watched plays at the Theatre of Dionysus on the Acropolis hillside.

questions.ask: A great navy of triremes
questions.fact: A trireme was a fast warship rowed by about 170 oarsmen in three rows.

questions.ask: Boys left home at 7 to train
questions.fact: Spartan boys lived in groups and trained to be soldiers in the agoge.

questions.ask: Ruled by two kings at once
questions.fact: Having two kings meant one could lead the army while the other stayed home.

questions.ask: Girls trained hard in sports
questions.fact: Spartan girls ran, wrestled and threw the javelin to keep strong.

questions.ask: Helots farmed the land
questions.fact: Helots were people forced to work the land, so Spartan citizens could train.

questions.ask: Warriors in red cloaks
questions.fact: Spartan soldiers were famous across Greece for their red cloaks and discipline.

questions.ask: Used iron bars as money
questions.fact: Heavy iron bars made it hard to get rich, as Spartans were meant to live simply.

quests.title: The First Olympics
quests.story: The crowd is roaring at Olympia! Step into the ancient stadium and discover how the very first Olympic Games were played.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the pot with the right answer.
quests.hint: Remember the Games were a festival for the Greek gods, held long before modern sports were invented.

questions.ask: Where were the ancient Olympic Games held?
questions.fact: Olympia was not a city but a holy site with temples, a stadium and training grounds.

questions.ask: When were the first Olympic Games recorded?
questions.fact: The Games were then held every four years for over a thousand years.

questions.ask: Which god were the Games held to honour?
questions.fact: A giant gold and ivory statue of Zeus at Olympia was a Wonder of the World.

questions.ask: What prize did an Olympic winner receive at the Games?
questions.fact: Back home, some cities gave winners free meals for the rest of their lives.

questions.ask: What was the short sprint, one length of the stadium, called?
questions.fact: It was about 192 metres long, and our word 'stadium' comes from it.

questions.ask: What was the pankration?
questions.fact: Its name means 'all strength' or 'all power' in Greek.

questions.ask: How many events were there in the pentathlon?
questions.fact: They were running, long jump, discus, javelin and wrestling.

questions.ask: In the chariot race, who was named the winner?
questions.fact: That is how Kyniska, a Spartan princess, became the first woman to win.

questions.ask: What was the Olympic truce?
questions.fact: It let athletes and fans travel safely to Olympia, even in times of war.

questions.ask: Who was allowed to compete in the ancient Olympic Games?
questions.fact: Women held their own games for the goddess Hera, called the Heraia.

questions.ask: What did athletes rub onto their skin before competing?
questions.fact: Afterwards they scraped off the oil and dust with a curved tool called a strigil.

questions.ask: In which year did the modern Olympic Games begin?
questions.fact: The first modern Games were held in Athens, Greece.

quests.title: Mount Olympus Mysteries

skill.name: Greek gods and what the Greeks gave us
skill.subject: history

quests.story: Thunder rumbles over Mount Olympus! Unroll the scrolls to meet the Greek gods and discover the ideas the Greeks gave the world.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the scroll with the right answer.
quests.hint: Think about Greek myths you know, and Greek ideas we still use in words, maths, sport and theatre.

questions.ask: Who did the Greeks believe was king of the gods?
questions.fact: The Greeks believed Zeus threw thunderbolts from his home on Mount Olympus.

questions.ask: Who did the Greeks believe was the god of the sea?
questions.fact: He was often shown holding a three-pronged spear called a trident.

questions.ask: Which goddess of wisdom was the protector of Athens?
questions.fact: Her symbol was the owl, which appeared on the coins of Athens.

questions.ask: In the famous myth, how did the Greeks get inside the city of Troy?
questions.fact: That's why a hidden trick is still called a 'Trojan horse' today.

questions.ask: What does the Greek word 'democracy' mean?
questions.fact: In Athens, male citizens voted on laws; women and enslaved people could not.

questions.ask: The word 'alphabet' comes from which two Greek letters?
questions.fact: Greek letters like pi (π) are still used in maths and science today.

questions.ask: Which Greek thinker is said to have shouted 'Eureka!' in his bath?
questions.fact: 'Eureka' means 'I have found it!'; he had worked out how to measure volume.

questions.ask: Which Greek mathematician is famous for a rule about triangles?
questions.fact: Pupils all over the world still learn Pythagoras' theorem in maths.

questions.ask: Which race is named after a legendary messenger's run?
questions.fact: The legend says a runner dashed about 25 miles from Marathon to Athens with news of victory.

questions.ask: Which two kinds of play did the Greeks invent?
questions.fact: Actors wore big masks so people at the back of huge open-air theatres could see.

questions.ask: Who did the Greeks believe ruled the underworld?
questions.fact: In the myths, a three-headed dog called Cerberus guarded its gates.

questions.ask: Where did the Greeks believe their gods lived?
questions.fact: Mount Olympus is a real mountain, the highest in Greece, nearly 3,000 metres tall.

quests.title: The Sutton Hoo Ship
quests.story: It's 1939 and something big is hidden under a grassy mound in Suffolk! Dig with Basil Brown to uncover an Anglo-Saxon king's treasure.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the mound with the right answer.
quests.hint: Think about an Anglo-Saxon king who was buried with his finest things, about 1,400 years ago.

questions.ask: In which English county is Sutton Hoo?
questions.fact: Sutton Hoo is near the town of Woodbridge, beside the River Deben.

questions.ask: Who began digging the great ship burial in 1939?
questions.fact: Basil Brown was a local self-taught archaeologist who also loved astronomy.

questions.ask: Who owned the land and asked for the mounds to be dug?
questions.fact: She gave the treasure to the British Museum, where you can still see it today.

questions.ask: What huge object was buried inside the biggest mound?
questions.fact: The wood had rotted away, but rows of iron rivets showed the ship's shape.

questions.ask: About how long was the Sutton Hoo ship?
questions.fact: That's longer than two double-decker buses parked end to end.

questions.ask: Who do most experts think was buried at Sutton Hoo?
questions.fact: The acid soil dissolved the body, so experts cannot be completely sure.

questions.ask: Which Anglo-Saxon kingdom did Rædwald rule?
questions.fact: Rædwald was a powerful king who had influence over other kingdoms too.

questions.ask: Which object with a face mask is Sutton Hoo's most famous find?
questions.fact: It was found in hundreds of pieces and put back together like a jigsaw.

questions.ask: What was the great gold buckle made to fasten?
questions.fact: Its hollow back opens up, so it may once have held something special.

questions.ask: About when was the ship burial made?
questions.fact: Gold coins found in a purse helped experts work out the date.

questions.ask: Which red gemstones decorate many of the gold treasures?
questions.fact: Thousands of tiny garnets were cut to fit, showing amazing Anglo-Saxon skill.

questions.ask: Which event began just weeks after the 1939 dig ended?
questions.fact: The treasure was kept safe in a London Underground tunnel during the war.

quests.title: Saxon Settlers

skill.name: Anglo-Saxon and Scots settlers in Britain
skill.subject: history

quests.story: The Romans have gone and new boats are landing on the shore! Unpack the crates and discover how the Anglo-Saxons and Scots made new homes.
quests.instruction: Read each question, then tap the crate with the right answer.
quests.hint: Think about farmers who crossed the sea after the Romans left, and the names and words they gave us.

questions.ask: About when did Anglo-Saxons begin to settle in Britain?
questions.fact: The Roman army had left around AD 410, and new settlers soon arrived.

questions.ask: Which three groups were the main Anglo-Saxon settlers?
questions.fact: The name England comes from 'Angle-land', the land of the Angles.

questions.ask: Where did the Anglo-Saxons come from?
questions.fact: They crossed the North Sea in long wooden boats rowed by oars.

questions.ask: Where did the Scots come from before settling in Scotland?
questions.fact: The Scots set up a kingdom called Dál Riata on the west coast of Scotland.

questions.ask: Which Anglo-Saxon kingdom covered much of the Midlands?
questions.fact: Other big kingdoms included Wessex, Northumbria and East Anglia.

questions.ask: What were Anglo-Saxon village homes made from?
questions.fact: A chief and his people feasted together in a large wooden hall.

questions.ask: What did the place-name ending '-ham' mean?
questions.fact: '-ton' meant a farm or settlement, as in Brighton or Taunton.

questions.ask: Who came from Rome in AD 597 to spread Christianity?
questions.fact: He became the first Archbishop of Canterbury, in the kingdom of Kent.

questions.ask: What were the letters of the early Anglo-Saxon alphabet called?
questions.fact: Runes were made of straight lines, which were easy to carve into wood or stone.

questions.ask: Which Anglo-Saxon poem tells of a hero who fights a monster?
questions.fact: Beowulf battles the monster Grendel and, later, a dragon.

questions.ask: How did most Anglo-Saxon people make a living?
questions.fact: Teams of oxen pulled heavy ploughs, and farmers grew wheat, barley and oats.

questions.ask: Which language did the Anglo-Saxons speak?
questions.fact: Everyday words like 'house', 'bread' and 'day' come from Old English.
